conceptTag: Read a software company's profit and loss
readerTitle: An 80% margin, and still losing money: reading a software company's numbers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (재고관리 소프트웨어 회사, 공구 소매 체인, 대기업 안의 소프트웨어 팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 소프트웨어 회사의 손익계산서는 매출총이익률로 '제품 자체가 돈을 버는지'를, 순이익률로 '성장에 얼마를 쓰는지'를 따로 읽어야 한다.
misconception: 매출총이익률이 80%면 돈을 잘 버는 회사이고, 적자면 제품이 나쁜 회사다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (손익계산서 구조, 매출원가, 매출총이익률, 순이익률)

factChecks.note: 가상 손익계산서 계산: 매출 $10M − 매출원가 $2M = 매출총이익 $8M(80%). 영업비용 $5M + $3M + $1.5M = $9.5M. $8M − $9.5M = −$1.5M(−15%). 이자와 세금은 단순화를 위해 생략했고 카드에도 밝혔습니다.
성장 중단 가정: 영업·마케팅 $5M → $2M이면 영업비용 $6.5M, $8M − $6.5M = +$1.5M(+15%). 실제로는 신규 판매가 줄고 일부 고객이 떠나 매출도 줄 수 있다는 점을 카드에 적었습니다.
사내 팀 사례: 매출 $3M, 매출원가 $1.5M → 매출총이익률 50%. 작년 65%는 가정값입니다.
'일반적인 소프트웨어 회사의 매출총이익률이 높다'는 일반론으로만 썼고 특정 평균 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 매출원가 분류가 회사마다 다르다는 점은 일반적 회계 관행 설명입니다.

cards.title: An 80% margin, and still losing money
body: A software company sells inventory tools to shops. For every $100 a customer pays, running the service costs it only $20.
Yet last year it lost $1.5 million. Both facts are true, and together they tell you more than either one alone.

image.label: A laptop showing a profit and loss report with one green and one red line
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노트북 화면에 손익계산서 한 장. 위쪽 줄 "Gross margin 80%"는 초록색, 맨 아래 줄 "Profit −$1.5M"은 빨간색. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're picking a software vendor.
body: You run a 12-store hardware chain and plan to sign a three-year deal for inventory software. The vendor shares its numbers: revenue up 50% to $10M, gross margin 80%, a loss of 15% of revenue.
What do these numbers tell you?

options.text: An 80% margin means they're very profitable
options.feedback: Gross margin only counts the cost of serving customers. It says nothing about the salaries and marketing below it, which is where this loss lives.

options.text: The product earns money per customer. Check what the spending below that line goes to
options.feedback: This is *gross vs net margin* at work. The high gross margin says the service itself pays; the net loss says they spend heavily elsewhere. You now know which question to ask.

options.text: They lose money, so pick a profitable vendor
options.feedback: A loss is worth noticing, but it doesn't say the product is broken. A loss from fast growth is very different from a loss from costly service.

cards.title: Read it top to bottom.
body: Interest and taxes are left out to keep it simple. The big gap opens below gross profit, not above it.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Revenue vs profit
cards.title: The top line grew. The bottom line didn't.
body: Revenue rose 50%, and that headline is what most vendors lead with. But **revenue** is only what customers paid. **Profit** is what remains after every cost.
Here, the faster the company grew, the more it spent to grow. A rising top line can sit on top of a flat or falling bottom line. So the first habit is simple: never stop reading at the first row.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Gross vs net margin
cards.title: Two margins, two different stories.
body: **Gross margin** (80%) answers: does serving a customer make money? Yes, clearly. The next customer costs little to run.
**Net margin** (−15%) answers: does the whole business make money? Not yet. Half of revenue goes to sales and marketing alone.
Read together, they point to one question. Is the company losing money because the product is costly, or because it's buying growth?

image.label: Two gauges: gross margin at 80%, net margin at minus 15%
image.brief: 계기판 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 "Gross margin 80%" 바늘은 초록 구간, 오른쪽 "Net margin −15%" 바늘은 빨간 구간. 두 계기판 사이에 "Sales & marketing $5M" 라벨이 붙은 화살표.

cards.title: What if growth slowed down?
body: Suppose the company cut sales and marketing from $5M to $2M. Operating costs would fall to $6.5M. With $8M of gross profit, a $1.5M loss becomes a $1.5M profit.

That's a rough test, not a forecast. Fewer new sales could also mean less revenue. But it shows the loss is mostly a choice to spend, not a product that can't pay for itself. For a vendor you'll rely on for three years, that matters.

cards.title: Check what's hiding in each line.
body: Companies don't all put the same costs in *cost of revenue*. One counts customer support and setup there. Another moves them into operating costs, which makes gross margin look higher.
So compare margins only after asking what each line contains. And a loss from growth is only reassuring if the company has the money to keep going until growth pays off.

cards.title: Now it's your own team's numbers.
body: You lead a team inside a larger company that sells a booking app to outside clinics. Revenue grew 40% to $3M. Cost of revenue was $1.5M, mostly staff who set up each clinic by hand. Last year your gross margin was 65%.
Your boss says: "Great growth. Let's double the team." What do you flag?

options.text: Nothing. 40% growth proves the plan works
options.feedback: That's reading only the top line. *Revenue vs profit*: growth that costs more to deliver can shrink what you keep.

options.text: Gross margin fell from 65% to 50%. Fix the manual setup before scaling
options.feedback: *Gross margin* shows each new clinic now costs more to serve. Doubling the team first would scale that problem.

options.text: Cut marketing to improve net margin
options.feedback: Net margin would look better, but the *gross margin* problem stays hidden underneath and grows with every new clinic.

cards.softwareNote: In software, a falling gross margin often means manual work is creeping in: hand-built setups, custom features or heavy support. It's an early warning before the bottom line shows it.

cards.title: Read the top line, then both margins.
body: You used two ideas: **revenue vs profit**, so a growth headline doesn't end your reading, and **gross vs net margin**, to separate what the product earns from what the business spends.
**Try it today:** take your own business's last profit and loss. Write your gross margin and net margin side by side, and name the one line that explains the gap.
